info.title: AI Code Tutorial Generator API
info.description: API for analyzing GitHub repos and generating tutorials.

post.description:
Add a repository to the caller's account.

Idempotent per user: submitting a URL already on the account returns the
existing row rather than erroring.

get.description:
List the caller's repositories.

Now paginated. The old version returned every repository the user owned in a
`{"repositories": [...]}` wrapper with no limit.

get.description:
Public catalogue for apps/site `/explore`. No authentication: this is the
growth channel (D8), and gating it walls off the crawler too.

Public tutorial by slug — the payload behind `/t/{slug}` on apps/site.

Public rows only; anything else is a plain 404 so the endpoint cannot be
used to confirm a private tutorial's slug exists.

Read a tutorial.

Optional auth: the owner sees their private tutorials, and anyone — signed in
or not — can read a public or unlisted one.

The previous version took no ownership into account *at all*. It fetched by
primary key and returned the whole body, so any authenticated user could read
any other user's tutorial. It also declared `response_model=Any`, so the
schema was absent from OpenAPI and nothing constrained what came back.

patch.description: Publish or unpublish. Owner only — visibility is not a read operation.

get.description: Raw pipeline output. Internal; use `GET /{tutorial_id}` to read a tutorial.

Server-Sent Events feed of pipeline step transitions.

**Auth is a ticket, not a header, on purpose.** `EventSource` cannot set an
Authorization header, and one-off `fetch`-based polyfills give up
auto-reconnect, which is most of the value of SSE. Instead the client takes
`stream_ticket` from an already-authenticated `GET /{instance_id}/status`
response and passes it here as a query parameter. The ticket is a JWT bound
to this instance *and* user, expires in `stream_ticket_expire_seconds` (120s
by default), and carries type `stream_ticket` — never accepted as a session
token, and a session token is never accepted as a ticket.

Rate limiting is deliberately not applied to this endpoint: it produces no
LLM work, and throttling heartbeats would break live updates. The
work-producing endpoints (`/generate`, `/{id}/retry`) are limited instead.

One caveat accepted and documented (docs/adr/): a ticket in a URL can leak
via referrer headers. The short expiry is the mitigation — a leaked URL is
dead in two minutes and only ever exposes step transitions, never content.

parameters.name: ticket

schema.description: Short-lived stream ticket from the status payload's `stream_ticket`.
schema.title: Ticket

parameters.description: Short-lived stream ticket from the status payload's `stream_ticket`.

post.description:
Register a new account.

Password length is enforced by the schema alone — the previous version
checked it in the schema *and* again in the handler, so the two could drift
apart and the duplicate was dead code.

Returns 201; the old handler created a resource and reported 200.

Exchange credentials for a token pair.

Still `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` (form-encoded, `username` field) because
that is what FastAPI's OAuth2 flow and the Swagger "Authorize" button expect,
and what the existing frontend already sends.

get.description:
The provider's consent-screen URL.

Returns JSON rather than a 302: the SPA needs the URL before it can decide
how to open it (same window, popup), and a redirect from an API endpoint is
awkward to consume from `fetch`.

The URL the provider redirects back to. Exchanges `code` and issues the
same token pair password login returns.

This endpoint is the redirect target, so the browser lands here with the
authorization code in the query string. `code` and `state` must never be
logged: the redaction filter in core/logging.py is defence in depth (it
scrubs `code=`/`state=` query shapes), and this handler deliberately does
not touch the request log at all.

An SPA in front of this wants the tokens handed to its own origin. It can
open the authorize URL directly in the top-level window, since this response
is JSON the browser will render — the documented flow is: frontend fetches
`/authorize` for the URL, navigates to it, and the provider's redirect lands
here, where the response carries the session the SPA then persists.

The authenticated user.

New. There was no way to ask "who am I" — the frontend faked it by calling
the *settings* endpoint and reconstructing a user object, which left
`id: undefined`, so the client never actually knew the user's id.

post.description: Mark a module finished. Idempotent — repeat calls keep the first timestamp.

post.description:
Grade an attempt, record the score, and mark the module complete.

The response carries `correct_answer` — after an attempt, which is the only
place it is disclosed. The quiz body itself never includes it; see
`schemas/tutorial.py::QuizOption`.

put.description:
`notification_id` is a `UUID` path parameter, so a malformed id is a 422
from FastAPI. The old handler took a `str`, parsed it by hand, and wrapped
everything in a `try/except Exception` that returned `str(e)` to the client.

delete.description: Dismiss. Previously the list could only grow.

get.description:
Substring search across the caller's repositories, tutorials, modules and
quizzes.

Scoped to the caller — this is not public discovery (that is `/explore` on
apps/site). A query shorter than two characters returns nothing, because
below the trigram threshold every table would be sequentially scanned.

Liveness: the process is up. Deliberately touches nothing external, so a
database blip cannot make the orchestrator restart a healthy container.

Readiness: dependencies are reachable. This is what a load balancer
should poll before routing traffic.

AccountDeleteRequest.title: AccountDeleteRequest
AccountDeleteRequest.description:
Deleting an account is irreversible and cascades to every tutorial the
user owns, so it re-authenticates rather than trusting the bearer token
alone. The old endpoint took no body at all.

ConnectedAccount.title: ConnectedAccount
ConnectedAccount.description:
**Read-only.** Server-managed, and no longer accepted on update.

It was writable, so a user could assert any linked account they liked —
including a GitHub identity they do not control. Nothing consumed it yet, but
OAuth (docs/DECISIONS.md D10) will, and a user-writable claim about identity
is a bad thing to inherit.

ExploreTutorialItem.title: ExploreTutorialItem
ExploreTutorialItem.description:
A public tutorial in the `/explore` catalogue (Phase 5.5).

Deliberately not `TutorialListItem`: that shape carries per-viewer progress
fields (`completed_modules`, `progress_percentage`) which have no meaning for
an anonymous visitor, and it has no `language`/`published_at`, which are the
two things a browse page is *for*. Separate model rather than a union of
optional fields — every field here is always present and meaningful.

GenerationStatusResponse.title: GenerationStatusResponse
GenerationStatusResponse.description:
Frontend-compatibility shape, camelCase and uppercase status.

Kept verbatim so the legacy client keeps working through the rewrite. It is
the one place uppercase status strings survive; everything else uses the
lowercase enum values.

LLMProvider.title: LLMProvider
LLMProvider.description:
Where a user's BYOK credential points.

CUSTOM covers any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (local Ollama, LiteLLM proxy, a
self-hosted gateway) — which is why `user_llm_credentials.base_url` exists.

OAuthAuthorizeResponse.title: OAuthAuthorizeResponse
OAuthAuthorizeResponse.description:
The consent-screen URL for one provider.

`state` is embedded in the URL (a signed JWT) rather than returned separately,
so the frontend cannot forget to pass it through — the CSRF protection is not
left to a caller's diligence.

OAuthProvider.title: OAuthProvider
OAuthProvider.description:
Login providers (D10a: password + GitHub + Google, all interchangeable).

Values are the URL slugs used in `/api/user/oauth/{provider}/...` and the
strings stored in `user_oauth_identities.provider`. That column is a plain
VARCHAR, not a PG enum, so adding a provider is a code change only — the
router validates against this enum before the value reaches the DB.

ProgressOverview.title: ProgressOverview
ProgressOverview.description:
Fixed-size dashboard payload.

The completion history used to be inlined here and was unbounded — it now
lives at `GET /api/progress/modules`, paginated.

QuizOption.title: QuizOption
QuizOption.description:
One selectable answer, **stripped of the answer key**.

`quizzes.options` is freeform JSONB and the option dicts written by
`routers/author.py` carry `is_correct` — that flag *is* the answer key
(`correct_answer` is derived from it, `quiz.correct_answer = the option whose
is_correct is true`).

Omitting the `correct_answer` column is therefore not enough on its own: the
old inline schema declared `options: list[dict]` and passed the raw JSONB
straight through, so every quiz shipped its own answer to the browser before
the question was attempted.

This model is an allowlist — `extra="ignore"` means any key not named below is
dropped on the way out, so a new answer-revealing field added to the JSON
later cannot leak by default. It fails closed.

QuizOptionInput.title: QuizOptionInput
QuizOptionInput.description:
An option as submitted by the author. `is_correct` is the answer key.

It is accepted here and stripped on the way out — see
`schemas/tutorial.py::QuizOption`.

QuizResult.title: QuizResult
QuizResult.description:
Returned after an attempt.

`correct_answer` is included **here and only here**. Revealing it in response
to a submission is the point of the feature; revealing it in the quiz body
beforehand is the leak (see `schemas/tutorial.py::QuizOption`).

RunStatus.title: RunStatus
RunStatus.description:
Shared by TutorialInstance, TutorialExecution and TutorialStepExecution.

One vocabulary for one concept — the three tables previously each declared
their own overlapping-but-not-identical set of strings.

TokenWithUser.title: TokenWithUser
TokenWithUser.description:
Login/refresh response. Bundling the user saves the client an immediate
follow-up request just to render a header.

TutorialUpdate.title: TutorialUpdate
TutorialUpdate.description:
All fields optional — this is a partial update.

`level` is typed as the enum rather than `str`. The old handler took a string,
called `.upper()` on it and wrote `"BEGINNER"`, which the `ck_tutorials_level`
CHECK constraint rejects — so every save including a level returned a 500.
Pydantic now rejects an unknown level with a 422 that names the field, and a
valid one can only be written in the stored lowercase form.

TutorialVisibility.title: TutorialVisibility
TutorialVisibility.description:
Public tutorials are the growth channel (see docs/DECISIONS.md D8).

Present from the first Phase 2 migration rather than retrofitted, because
adding it later would mean touching the auth model, the router, the schema
and apps/site simultaneously.

UnreadCountResponse.title: UnreadCountResponse
UnreadCountResponse.description:
Its own endpoint so a bell badge can poll the count without pulling a
page of notification bodies every few seconds.

UserPublic.title: UserPublic
UserPublic.description: A user as returned to that user. Never includes password material.

app__schemas__author__QuizResponse.title: QuizResponse
app__schemas__author__QuizResponse.description:
The authoring view — the owner wrote the answer key, so it is returned.

This is why it is a separate model from `schemas/tutorial.py::QuizResponse`,
which is the *learner* view and strips it.
